scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

He says he feels territorial and gets agitated when women he's friends with talk to or get attention from other guys. He compares it to not wanting to put himself through unnecessary discomfort outside of work, where he has to tolerate these feelings. He also mentions that if a woman is his girlfriend, he doesn't mind her interacting with others because he knows she's his. So, it seems like his issue is more about potential romantic feelings or possessiveness rather than genuine friendship. On the other hand, the woman he's talking to just wants to be friends and go out for drinks. She didn't seem to have any romantic intentions, just wanted to hang out as friends. When he told her he doesn't do friendships with women, she suggested he see a psychologist, which he dismissed. Since then, their conversations have become strictly work-related. Now, is it right or wrong for him to be honest about his feelings? On one hand, honesty is important in relationships, whether they're romantic or platonic. If he's uncomfortable with the situation, it's better to communicate that rather than pretending everything is fine. On the other hand, his honesty might have come across as dismissive or even controlling, which could be off-putting to the woman. I also need to consider the societal norms around friendships between men and women. There's often an assumption that any close interaction between a man and a woman could be romantic, which can put pressure on both parties. The guy might be overthinking or projecting his insecurities onto the situation, which isn't fair to the woman who just wants to be friends. Another angle is the impact of his honesty on their working relationship. By being so open about his discomfort, he might have created an awkward or tense environment at work, which isn't ideal for either of them. It's possible that his honesty, while well-intentioned, has had unintended negative consequences. I also wonder about his suggestion to see a psychologist. He dismissed it, saying his flaws are part of who he is. While it's okay to have flaws, if these feelings are causing him significant distress or affecting his relationships, it might be worth exploring them further. In terms of whether it's right or wrong, I think it's more about the approach rather than the honesty itself. Being honest is good, but the way he delivered it might have been insensitive or misinterpreted. It's possible that he could have communicated his boundaries in a more respectful and less personal way, without making the woman feel judged or dismissed. Overall, while honesty is important, the manner in which it's delivered and the context in which it's received play a crucial role.
